system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a history of coronary artery disease, prior CABG, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and a previous stroke was admitted after a mechanical fall at home two days prior. She reported no loss of consciousness or pre-syncopal symptoms but described chronic dizziness and gait instability. Evaluation included a normal head CT and EKG, negative cardiac enzymes, and no orthostatic hypotension, ruling out acute neurological or cardiac causes. She was found to have contusions to the head, shoulder, and leg but no fractures. Physical therapy recommended a cane and outpatient rehabilitation for balance and strength. Her diabetes was poorly controlled with admission glucose in the 200s and a recent A1c of 8.5%; her insulin regimen was simplified to 70/30 insulin twice daily with sliding scale coverage. She was discharged home with instructions to use a cane, attend physical therapy, adhere to her new insulin regimen, and follow up with her primary care provider.
problems: Contusion of unspecified part of lower limb
Fall from other slipping, tripping, or stumbling
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Personal history of transient ischemic attack (TIA), and cerebral infarction without residual deficits

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was cleaning my kitchen and suddenly felt a tightness in my chest. It went to my left shoulder and I had trouble catching my breath. I took two nitroglycerin tablets and it helped a little, but didn’t go away completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And then it happened again yesterday evening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, when I ran into my ex-mother-in-law—startled me! The pain came back and lasted a while. That’s when I called for help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds stressful. We’ve checked several things. Your EKG was stable, no new changes, and your cardiac enzymes—like troponin—were negative. That means there’s no sign of a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. But why am I still having pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your chest X-ray shows no pneumonia or fluid, but we did notice some tenderness when pressing on your chest wall. That, along with your normal heart tests, makes us think this is costochondritis— inflammation where your ribs attach to the breastbone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart? But I’ve had bypass surgery before and stents… I was really worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I completely understand. Given your history—CABG, stents, diabetes, high blood pressure—we take any chest pain very seriously. But your previous catheterization showed your grafts are still working, and your heart function is good. This pain seems musculoskeletal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the treatment? More morphine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch to acetaminophen—Tylenol—for the pain. It’s safer and effective for this kind of inflammation. We’re not using NSAIDs like naproxen right now because of your history of stomach ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My blood pressure was high last time I was here—am I still on all my heart meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we restarted your amlodipine, lisinopril, and chlorthalidone. Your blood pressure is now in the 130s, much better than the 160s when you arrived. We think it was high due to missing doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I admit I’ve been skipping a few. Too many pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. But they’re important—especially with your history. We’re keeping your insulin, metformin, atorvastatin, and all your other usual medications the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your labs came back. Your kidney function and electrolytes are stable, and your blood sugar this morning was 76, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my A1C? Last time it was 8.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still 8.5, but trending down. We’ll keep you on the 70/30 insulin twice daily with sliding scale as needed. Your diabetes team can help fine-tune it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is better, and your vitals are stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What should I do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking Tylenol for the chest wall pain. Continue all your regular medications. And please follow up with your primary doctor and cardiologist in the next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I use the nitroglycerin if the chest pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you’re unsure whether it’s heart-related. But if the pain is reproducible by pressing on your chest, it’s likely the same inflammation. Call us if it gets worse or you have shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my asthma? I’ve been using my inhaler more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve kept you on your Advair and albuterol as needed. Use the inhaler regularly, especially if you feel tightness. But your lungs sounded clear today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’ll go home with a walker for stability—given your recent fall history—and instructions to avoid heavy lifting until the chest pain resolves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing it’s not my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a history of coronary artery disease, prior CABG, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and a previous stroke was admitted for evaluation of substernal chest pain radiating to the left shoulder, occurring during physical activity and emotional stress. Initial concerns for acute coronary syndrome were ruled out by normal cardiac enzymes, unchanged EKG, and no acute findings on chest X-ray. The pain was reproducible on chest wall palpation, leading to a diagnosis of costochondritis. Her blood pressure was elevated on admission, likely due to medication noncompliance, and improved with reinitiation of home antihypertensives. She remained on her baseline medications for diabetes, hyperlipidemia, asthma, and depression. She was discharged home with instructions to use acetaminophen for pain, continue all chronic medications, and follow up with her primary care provider and cardiologist.
